name: Death
up: Inevitable transformation and endings. The threshold between life and death at Samhain. Necessary completion before new beginning. The harvest's final cutting. Acceptance of mortality and change. The dark rider who announces transformation.
rev: Fear of change preventing necessary endings. Clinging to what must die. Transformation resisted. Stagnation through fear of death/change. Refusing to cross the threshold.
myth: The Dullahan is a headless horseman of Irish folklore who appears at Samhain. He carries his own severed head which sees all. When he stops riding, someone dies - he calls their name and they must go. He represents death as inevitable transformation, the necessary ending that allows new life.

name: Judgement
up: The call to transformation and crossing thresholds. Ancestral voices calling you to your destiny. Awakening to higher purpose. The keen that announces rebirth. Judgment of life lived and preparation for what comes next. Samhain's transformative power.
rev: Ignoring the call of destiny. Fear of transformation preventing growth. Refusing to face judgment of one's actions. The ancestral cry unheeded. Denying necessary endings.
myth: The Bean Sídhe ('woman of the fairy mound') appears to families to keen for their dying, her cry announcing a death. She's not an omen of evil but a psychopomp calling souls to the Otherworld. She represents necessary transitions, the judgment of life lived, and the call to transformation.

name: Justice
up: Like the Brehon laws that governed Celtic society with intricate fairness, this is the principle of balance and right action woven into the fabric of existence. The Celts understood justice not as abstract morality but as the maintenance of cosmic order - each person receiving their due, debts balanced, harmony restored. The scales are in balance; truth prevails over deception. What is fair will be done, not through mercy but through the inexorable workings of natural law.
rev: The scales tip unfairly, laws are applied unjustly, truth is obscured by falsehood. Like a corrupt judge taking bribes or a witness giving false testimony, the mechanisms of justice have been corrupted. The Celtic tradition held that such imbalance would eventually correct itself - for the universe itself demands equilibrium - but the process may be painful and slow. Seek the truth even when systems fail to recognize it.
myth: Connected to the Brehon legal system and the concept of "fír flathemon" (truth of the ruler) - the belief that a just king would cause the land itself to prosper, while injustice would bring blight and disaster.

name: Strength
up: Mastery through discipline and inner strength. The warrior woman who trains heroes. Gentle power that tames the fierce. Teaching and transformation through challenge. Courage combined with compassion. The strength found on Scáthach's isle of warriors.
rev: Brutality masquerading as strength. Failure to control one's power. Weakness hidden by aggression. Training that breaks rather than builds. Compassion without necessary firmness.
myth: Scáthach ('The Shadowy One'), legendary Scottish warrior woman who trained heroes including Cú Chulainn on the Isle of Skye. She taught not just combat skills but emotional control and spiritual strength. Her training ground (Dún Scáith) was a place of transformation where boys became heroes.

name: Temperance
up: Balance and healing through sacred fire and water. Tempering the sword in Brigid's forge. Unity of opposites - fire and ice, poetry and smithcraft. Gentle transformation through patience. Healing arts and the balanced life. Imbolc's promise of spring returning.
rev: Imbalance between opposing forces. Healing delayed or refused. Extremes without moderation. Creative fire burnt out or frozen. Sacred balance disturbed.
myth: Brigid, triple goddess of fire - smith, poet, and healer. She balances opposing forces and transforms through her sacred flame. Her holy wells flow with healing waters while her forge creates powerful weapons. Patron of Imbolc when winter begins its transformation to spring. She represents perfect balance and gentle transformation.

name: The Chariot
up: Victory through controlled battle-fury. The warrior who defends the threshold. Triumph of will and skill. Harnessing opposing forces (warp-spasm controlled). Swift action and determination. The champion who stands alone against armies at Lughnasadh harvest.
rev: Reckless battle-rage without control. Victory at too high a cost. Inability to balance opposing forces. Aggression that serves no purpose. Warrior's pride leading to downfall.
myth: Cú Chulainn, Ulster's greatest hero, who single-handedly defended his homeland against Queen Medb's armies. His warp-spasm (ríastrad) transformed him into an unstoppable force. Named 'Hound of Culann,' he represents controlled ferocity and heroic dedication.

name: The Devil
up: Confronting the shadow and destructive forces. Tyranny and oppression that must be faced. Material bondage and unhealthy attachments. The poisonous eye that destroys what it sees. Power of fear and the chains we forge ourselves.
rev: Breaking free from bondage and toxic patterns. Overcoming the destructive gaze. Liberation from fear and oppression. The giant finally defeated. Recognizing false power.
myth: Balor, king of the Fomorians (demons of chaos), possessed an evil eye that destroyed all it gazed upon. His eye was so heavy that four men lifted its lid with hooks. He represents tyranny, darkness, and the destructive forces that oppose order. His grandson Lugh eventually slew him, representing light overcoming darkness.

name: The Emperor
up: Rightful sovereignty and just rule. Protection of the realm through strength and wisdom. The sacred king who maintains balance. Order established through honor and the oath-bond. Leadership that serves the people and land.
rev: Tyranny and abuse of power. Kingship without the land's blessing. Rigid control that stifles growth. Authority without wisdom or compassion. The wounded king whose land suffers.
myth: Arthur Pendragon, the once and future king who drew the sword from the stone. His sovereignty was blessed by the Lady of the Lake, connecting earthly and Otherworldly authority. The Round Table represents equal justice. His reign symbolizes the golden age when king and land are one.

name: The Empress
up: Sovereignty of the land and abundance. Divine motherhood and fertility. The greening of spring at Beltane. Nurturing power that brings forth life. Connection to horses and swift movement between worlds. Generous provision and earthly pleasures.
rev: Smothering love or neglect. Abundance withheld or wasted. Disconnection from the land's rhythms. Fertility blocked. Over-attachment to material comfort.
myth: Rhiannon, Welsh goddess of horses, sovereignty, and the Otherworld. Her magical birds could wake the dead and lull the living to sleep. She represents the generous, nurturing aspect of the land itself, blessing those who honor her with abundance. Her white horse moves between mortal and immortal realms.

name: The Fool
up: Beginning a journey into the Otherworld (Annwn). Pure potential and innocent trust in the path ahead. The threshold moment before Samhain when veils are thin. Stepping forward with faith despite uncertainty, as Pwyll did when he accepted the year-long exchange with Arawn.
rev: Recklessness without wisdom. Ignoring omens and ancestral warnings. Foolishness rather than sacred innocence. Missing the lessons the Otherworld offers. Naivety that dishonors the sacred journey.
myth: Pwyll ventured unknowingly into Annwn (the Welsh Otherworld) while hunting, meeting Arawn, King of Annwn. His innocent acceptance of a year-long body-swap demonstrates the Fool's willingness to step into the unknown. Associated with Samhain (Oct 31-Nov 1), when the veil between worlds is thinnest and new journeys begin.

name: The Hanged Man
up: Sacrifice and transformation between worlds. Hanging in limbo, neither living nor dead. Gaining wisdom through suspension and surrender. The solar hero wounded and reborn. Seeing from a different perspective. The necessary pause before transformation.
rev: Meaningless suffering without transformation. Refusing the sacrifice that leads to rebirth. Stuck between worlds without purpose. Victim mentality. Self-martyrdom without wisdom gained.
myth: Lleu Llaw Gyffes ('Bright One of the Skillful Hand') was cursed by his mother Arianrhod and later transformed into an eagle after being wounded. Found hanging in an oak tree between life and death, he was restored by Gwydion. His story embodies death and resurrection, sacrifice and transformation.

name: The Hermit
up: Withdrawal to seek inner wisdom. The mad prophet who sees truth in solitude. Finding clarity in the wild places. Wisdom gained through suffering and retreat. The seer who dwells in the forest between worlds. Samhain's introspective darkness.
rev: Isolation that leads to madness rather than wisdom. Refusing to share knowledge gained. Hermitage as escape rather than seeking. Prophecy ignored or misunderstood. Lost in the wilderness without purpose.
myth: Myrddin Wyllt fled to the Caledonian Forest after witnessing the horror of battle, gaining prophetic visions in his wilderness madness. Living wild among the trees and animals, he became an oracle sought by kings. His isolation brought him closer to the Otherworld's truths than any court magician.

name: The Hierophant
up: Like the Druids who held the sacred knowledge and initiated seekers into ancient mysteries, this is the guardian of tradition and spiritual wisdom. The Hierophant stands at the threshold between the mundane and the sacred, teaching those who would learn the old ways. Celtic society revered those who preserved and transmitted sacred knowledge through generations. Seek legitimate spiritual guidance; respect the tested wisdom of tradition while remaining open to genuine understanding.
rev: The teacher has become dogmatic, preferring rigid rules over living wisdom. Like a Druid who recites formulas without understanding their meaning, or a Christian monk who values tradition over truth. The Celtic tradition valued wisdom over mere learning, understanding over rote memorization. Question authorities who demand blind obedience; true spiritual teaching liberates rather than constrains.
myth: Represents the Druids, the priestly class of Celtic society who spent decades in training, memorizing vast bodies of sacred knowledge, law, poetry, and performing religious ceremonies and initiations.

name: The High Priestess
up: Divine feminine wisdom and prophecy. Understanding the mysteries between life and death. Keeper of fate's threads. Intuition that sees beyond the veil. The dark moon wisdom that reveals hidden truths at Samhain.
rev: Hidden enemies and unclear prophecies. Using mystical knowledge to manipulate. Secrets kept that should be revealed. Feminine power turned destructive. Refusing to see what is shown.
myth: The Morrígan is the triple goddess of war, fate, and sovereignty. She appears to heroes as a washer at the ford, predicting their deaths. Guardian of sacred mysteries and chooser of the slain. Her crow form connects her to Otherworldly wisdom and the secrets of death and rebirth.

name: The Lovers
up: Sacred union and fated love. The choice between passion and duty. Bonds forged by love potion or geis (sacred obligation). Beltane's fire of desire. The joining that transforms both partners. Love that transcends ordinary boundaries.
rev: Forbidden love causing harm. Betrayal of oaths through passion. Choices made from lust rather than true connection. Love triangle's pain. Passion without wisdom or honor.
myth: The tragic lovers bound by a magical love potion. Their story exemplifies the Celtic concept of geis (binding fate) and the conflict between personal desire and social duty. Their love burned bright as Beltane fires but could not exist within the mortal world's constraints.

name: The Magician
up: Mastery of the four treasures of the Tuatha Dé Danann. Manifestation through will and knowledge. Druidic power to shape reality. Connection between earthly and Otherworldly realms. The skill to work with natural forces during the turning of seasons.
rev: Manipulation and trickery. Using knowledge for selfish gain. Breaking sacred oaths. Misuse of magical power. Charlatanism rather than true druidic wisdom.
myth: Merlin (Myrddin Emrys) embodies the archetypal Celtic wizard who bridges worlds and masters transformation. His tools represent the four treasures of the Tuatha Dé Danann: the Sword of Light, the Spear of Lugh, the Cauldron of Dagda, and the Stone of Fál. Associated with Imbolc (Feb 1-2), the fire festival of inspiration and magic.

name: The Moon
up: Mystery and shapeshifting between worlds. Illusion and the liminal space between sea and land. Instinct and the subconscious depths. The pull of the tides and lunar cycles. Hidden nature and secret selves. Dreams and the Otherworld's call.
rev: Deception and false appearances. Unable to return to true form. Lost between worlds. Confusion and madness from lunar influence. Secrets kept too long. Fear of transformation.
myth: Selkies are seal-folk who shed their skins to become human on land. They live between two worlds, never fully belonging to either. If their sealskin is hidden, they're trapped on land. They represent the mysterious, the hidden self, and the pull of the unknown. Their dual nature embodies the Moon's mystery and transformation.

name: The Star
up: Hope and renewal after darkness. The beautiful star-maiden restored. Healing waters poured forth. Faith in rebirth and transformation. Beauty that survives through all trials. The first star of evening bringing promise. Spring's eventual return after winter.
rev: Lost hope or faith. Beauty and grace tarnished. Healing delayed. Disconnection from divine guidance. The star obscured by clouds. Despair blocking renewal.
myth: Étaín, transformed multiple times through jealousy - from woman to pool to worm to fly to woman again. Despite her ordeals, she retained her beauty and grace. She represents hope that survives transformation, the star that guides through darkness. Her story is one of eventual restoration and rebirth after suffering.

name: The Sun
up: Brilliance and mastery of all skills. The many-skilled god at the height of his power. Success, vitality, and clear vision. Lughnasadh harvest and summer's peak. Joy and accomplishment. Light that dispels all darkness and doubt.
rev: Arrogance in skill. Burnt out or exhausted by trying to do everything. Success that brings hollow victory. Skills wasted or misdirected. Light too harsh, lacking shadow's wisdom.
myth: Lugh Lámhfhada ('Long Arm'), the many-skilled god who mastered every craft and art. He led the Tuatha Dé Danann to victory over the Fomorians and slew his grandfather Balor. Lughnasadh celebrates his foster-mother Tailtiu and the first harvest. He represents peak achievement, skill, and the sun's full power.

name: The Tower
up: Sudden destruction of false structures. The giant's bridge destroyed by its creator's fear. Revelations that shatter illusions. Necessary collapse that clears space for truth. Pride's downfall. The crumbling of what was built on false foundations.
rev: Avoiding necessary destruction. Clinging to crumbling structures. Delaying inevitable collapse. Fear of chaos preventing growth. Rebuilding on the same false foundations.
myth: Legend tells that Fionn mac Cumhaill built the Giant's Causeway to Scotland to fight the giant Benandonner. When he saw how huge his opponent was, he disguised himself as a baby. Benandonner fled in terror, destroying the causeway behind him. The story represents pride's downfall and structures destroyed by their creator's realization of folly.

name: The World
up: Completion and perfect union with the land. Sovereignty achieved and wholeness realized. The wheel's full turn through all seasons. Ireland herself embodied. Integration of all elements and lessons. The dance of perfect balance and fulfillment.
rev: Incomplete journey or denied sovereignty. Disconnection from the land. Wholeness sought but not achieved. The wheel stuck before completion. Crown refused or sovereignty withdrawn.
myth: Ériu, goddess who gave her name to Ireland (Éire). She and her sisters (Banba and Fódla) are sovereignty goddesses who embody the land itself. The rightful king must achieve sacred marriage with the sovereignty goddess to rule justly. She represents the completion of the cycle, the land in perfect balance, and the achievement of wholeness.

name: Wheel of Fortune
up: The turning of fate's wheel through the seasons. Silver wheel of the heavens and time's passage. Destiny's inevitable changes. The spiral castle between worlds. Fortune rises and falls as the year turns. Acceptance of life's cycles and cosmic order.
rev: Fighting against fate's turning. Bad luck or karmic consequences. The wheel stuck or broken. Refusing to accept necessary change. Destiny denied or perverted.
myth: Arianrhod ('Silver Wheel'), Welsh goddess of the stars, time, and fate. Her spiral castle, Caer Arianrhod, sits between mortal world and Otherworld. She spins the wheel of the heavens and determines destiny. Mother of Lleu Llaw Gyffes, she placed tynghedau (fates/destinies) upon him.
